activities.anchor: three relationships do all the work
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the transversal's three relationships
activities.name: geoParallelCloze

config.text: Parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles are equal (the %%0%%-shape), alternate angles are equal (the %%1%%-shape), and co-interior angles sum to %%2%% (the C-shape).
config.hint: Two letters that look like the angle patterns, and the straight-line total.

config.prompt: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n − 2) × 180°. Roughly what is the sum for a hexagon?
config.why: (6 − 2) × 180° = 720° — 180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral, 540° for a pentagon, 720° for a hexagon.
config.context: draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side and the triangle's angles rearrange into a straight line

config.root: Two triangles share two sides and a non-included angle (ASS). Are they congruent?

choices.label: Yes — three facts always pin a triangle down
choices.feedback: Not these three: ASS famously does not work — two different triangles can share two sides and a non-included angle.

choices.label: No — only SSS, SAS and ASA (plus RHS) guarantee congruence
choices.feedback: Right: the included angle is what pins the third side down; a non-included angle leaves the shape ambiguous.

choices.label: Yes, if the shared angle is a right angle
choices.feedback: That is RHS — right angle, hypotenuse, side — the one special case that does work.

trap.text: Three facts are enough only when they are the right three facts.

works.text: SSS, SAS and ASA each include the information that fixes the triangle's shape.

rhs.text: The right angle removes the ambiguity — which is why RHS is a special case worth keeping.

config.why: Congruence needs the right three facts: SSS, SAS, ASA (plus RHS) — and ASS is the famous near-miss.

activities.anchor: A dog twice the size of a terrier
activities.caption: call the weight of twice the size
activities.name: geoScaleEst

config.prompt: A dog twice the size of a terrier (scale factor k = 2) is how many times as heavy?
config.why: Volumes scale by k³ — 2³ = 8 — which is why elephants need thick legs while ants do not: weight grows as the cube, bone strength as the square.
config.context: lengths multiply by k, areas by k², volumes by k³

activities.anchor: A worked taste of the method
activities.caption: find the backwards theorem
activities.name: geoTangentSpot

config.prompt: One of these circle theorems is misstated — click it:
lines: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 45°.
config.correction: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact — 90°, not 45°.
config.why: The radius is the shortest line to the circle, so it must meet the tangent at 90°.

activities.anchor: Label the vertices A, B, C, D
activities.caption: rebuild the cyclic-quadrilateral proof
activities.name: geoCyclicOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the proof that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180° — what comes first:
items: The angle at the centre standing on that arc is twice angle ADC
The reflex centre angle is twice angle ABC, which stands on the other arc
config.why: Two applications of one theorem and an instant corollary — and the proof never measured anything. That is the payoff of the Euclidean method: many facts from one argument.

activities.caption: hyperbolic or elliptic — file each claim
activities.name: geoNonEuclidSort

config.prompt: File each claim under the non-Euclidean geometry it describes:

items.label: infinitely many parallels through the point
triangle angles sum to less than 180°
on a sphere, triangle angles can exceed 180°

config.why: The parallel postulate is not a truth of logic but a choice — and the universe we live in turns out to have made a non-Euclidean one, which GPS satellites correct for daily.
